title: 2024 Smart-Meter Electricity Consumption — Verified Findings Report
executive_summary: In 2024 the portfolio's 12 smart meters logged 1,428 readings totalling 1,207,699.96 kWh (average 845.73 kWh per reading). Industrial sites drove demand at 995,362.16 kWh, about 82.4% of all energy. Consumption peaked in Q4 (352,881.81 kWh) and bottomed out in Q3 (264,863.12 kWh); second-half usage rose 4.71% versus the first half. Peak-tariff energy accounted for 49.65% of usage — an almost even split with off-peak. Commercial sites averaged 415.29 kWh on hot days, and commercial consumption correlated moderately negatively with temperature (-0.638). The single busiest meter supplied about 20.9% of total energy.

key_findings.statement: Across 2024, the cleaned dataset contains 1,428 smart-meter readings totalling 1,207,699.96 kWh, an average of 845.73 kWh per reading.
Industrial buildings dominate consumption with 995,362.16 kWh (about 82.4% of total), far ahead of Commercial at 196,367.15 kWh (16.3%) and Residential at 15,970.65 kWh (1.3%).
Quarterly consumption ranked Q4 highest (352,881.81 kWh), then Q1 (319,677.67 kWh), Q2 (270,277.36 kWh) and Q3 lowest (264,863.12 kWh); Q4 rebounded 33.2% above the Q3 trough.
Consumption in July-December (617,744.93 kWh) increased 4.71% versus January-June (589,955.03 kWh), a gain of 27,789.90 kWh in the second half.
On hot days (temperature_c >= 25), Commercial sites recorded 19 readings averaging 415.29 kWh — roughly 0.49 times the overall per-reading average of 845.73 kWh.

Consumption is strongly right-skewed: the median reading is 406.8 kWh while the mean is 845.73 kWh (about 2.08 times the median), with a sample standard deviation of 913.44 kWh. Mean observed temperature was 11.61 C, with 62 readings missing temperature. For Commercial readings, temperature and energy correlate at -0.638, a moderate negative relationship.

Off-peak consumption (608,075.89 kWh) slightly exceeded peak (599,624.07 kWh) by 8,451.82 kWh, with peak energy representing 49.65% of the total. The portfolio spans 12 unique meters; the highest-use single meter consumed 252,241.26 kWh, about 20.9% of all energy.

limitations: Temperature is missing for 62 readings; hot-day and correlation analyses exclude them, which may bias those results.
Only 19 hot-day Commercial readings were observed, so the 415.29 kWh hot-day mean rests on a small sample.
Residential volume is very small (15,970.65 kWh), so building-type comparisons largely reflect meter deployment, not sector efficiency.
The Commercial temperature-energy correlation (-0.638) is associational, not causal, and may be confounded by seasonality or occupancy patterns.
Data cover only 2024 and 12 meters; findings may not generalise to other years or sites.
conclusion: Industrial sites and the Q1/Q4 winter peak should anchor efficiency and capacity planning. With peak and off-peak usage nearly equal (49.65% peak), tariff optimisation offers modest upside. Before setting firm targets, we recommend broadening residential metering, closing temperature data gaps, and adding multi-year data.
